extracted.intended_audience: experimental physicists / instrument makers / readers of Nature (scientists interested in thermometry and electrical measurement)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and using thermometric instruments that measure temperature via the change of electrical resistance in conductors, including remote/inaccessible measurements and high-temperature pyrometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electrical resistance as temperature index
rubrics_metrics.description: The conductivity (electrical resistance) of a wire is greatly influenced by its temperature; the law of increase of electrical resistance with temperature provides an index analogous to gas expansion and can be used to measure temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is the basis of the instrument presented: substitute 'electrical resistance in conductors' for 'expansion of gases'. The effect is progressive with temperature and was previously developed by Arndsen, Swanberg, Lenz, and Werner Siemens. Practical apparatus and calibration are required to exploit this law for accurate thermometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air thermometer as theoretical ideal (but impractical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expansion of a permanent gas at constant pressure is a most perfect index of temperature (Galileo's air thermometer principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The air thermometer is a 'universal thermometer' in principle and theoretically reaches absolute zero by Charles's law, but in practice it is inconvenient: indications must be corrected for barometric variations; the capacity of the descending tube (air not subjected to temperature change) must be accounted for; reliable observations require special experimental precautions accessible mainly to experimental physicists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential coil comparison method for remote/inaccessible temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the temperature of a distant or inaccessible place by comparing the electrical resistance of two matched coils (one at the unknown location, one in a comparison bath) using a differential galvanometer to detect balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure demonstrated by placing one coil in the subject (e.g., a hand) and the other in iced water, then adding warm water until no deflection is observed; the comparison bath's thermometer then gives the remote temperature. Applicable to physiological measurements, interior of cargoes, elevated points, or great depths; limited by the achievable temperature range of the comparison bath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-wire compensation to eliminate lead-wire resistance error
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove errors from the resistance of long leading wires, unite three insulated leading wires into a cable forming two galvanic circuits so that variations in resistance of the leading wires affect both sides of the balance equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One circuit passes through the distant spiral and back by one wire; the other passes through the near coil and up to the distant coil without traversing it, returning by the same return wire. Both circuits include the leading wires up to the distant coil so temperature-induced variations in those wires cancel out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material choice: platinum for high-temperature coils
rubrics_metrics.description: Platinum is the only suitable metal for coils intended to resist intense heats without deteriorating through fusion or oxidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even platinum deteriorates if exposed directly to flame and therefore requires external protection, insulation, and a support material that will not fuse or become conductive at high temperatures. Design must account for platinum's strengths and vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical construction: coil wound on hard-baked porcelain with insulating features
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin platinum wire should be coiled upon a hard-baked porcelain cylinder with a double-threaded helical groove to prevent contact between turns; the cylinder is pierced for passage of thick platinum leading wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porcelain provides insulation and mechanical support; projecting rims separate the spiral from the surrounding protecting tube. The design includes a longitudinal loop and binding screw for adjustment, and thicker platinum leads that connect to the thin spiral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective outer tube and handle; choice of protective metal by temperature range
rubrics_metrics.description: Surround the sensitive spiral with a protecting tube (platinum recommended) joined to a longer tube of wrought iron serving as a handle; for temperatures not exceeding moderate white heat (~1,300°C) the lower protecting tube may be wrought iron to save expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protecting tube shields the spiral from direct flame and oxidation; material selection balances cost and temperature resistance (wrought iron for ≤~1300°C, platinum for higher). The lower portion up to the conical enlargement is the part exposed to heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for resistance (zero) adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a longitudinal loop and a movable platinum binding screw in the upper portion of the porcelain cylinder to permit adjustment of the instrument's electrical resistance at the zero of the Centigrade scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanical adjustment allows calibration to set the baseline resistance corresponding to 0°C, improving accuracy and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirements for an absolute electrical pyrometer
rubrics_metrics.description: A pyrometer relying on absolute measurement of electrical resistance must use a coil that resists intense heat without deterioration, be properly insulated and supported, and neutralise the influence of leading wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving absolute pyrometry requires durable high-temperature materials (platinum), protective construction, three-wire compensation (or equivalent) for lead-wire effects, and careful calibration. Without these, measurements at very high temperatures will be unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction for deep-sea temperature coils
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep-sea measuring coils are made by winding a large quantity of insulated copper or iron wire upon a metallic tube open at both ends so sea-water can impart its temperature to innermost layers; the coil is externally protected by a vulcanised india-rubber tube bound by a close spiral layer of copper wire to exclude seawater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement allows the sea-water to reach inner layers for accurate sensing while preventing water ingress into the sensitive coil; suitable insulation and external protection are necessary for durability and accurate deep-sea readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of differential galvanometer with optical amplification for sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a differential galvanometer whose needle deflections are projected by mirror and lens onto a screen (illuminated by an electric lamp) so that small balance changes between the two branches (heated vs cooler coils) are visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This optical amplification permits detection of slight resistance imbalances when the two branch resistances are nearly equal; practical for demonstrations and sensitive laboratory measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of limitations and suitable applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The electrical-resistance comparison method is well-suited for moderate temperature remote measurements (physiology, cargoes, meteorology) but is limited by the temperature range of the comparison bath and by material constraints for very high temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inaccessible places where the comparison-bath method suffices, the technique offers non-invasive and continuous measurement. For furnace-level or higher temperatures, a protected platinum coil pyrometer and absolute resistance measurement are required; care must be taken to avoid deterioration and to account for lead-wire effects.
